title: Ramanujan knew on the spot why taxi number 1729 was anything but dull
body: G. H. Hardy once visited Srinivasa Ramanujan, who was ill in hospital, and remarked that his taxi’s number, 1729, seemed a rather dull one. No, said Ramanujan: it is a very interesting number, **the smallest expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways**. The exchange gave mathematics the term taxicab number, for the smallest integer that is a sum of two positive cubes in a given number of ways. Yet 1729 appears in a Ramanujan notebook dated years earlier, and Frénicle de Bessy had noted the property in 1657.

slides.text: I had ridden in taxi cab No. 1729 and remarked that the number seemed to me rather a dull one... ‘No,’ he replied, ‘it is a very interesting number; it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.’

slides.prompt: 1729 = 1³ + 12³. What is the other way to write it as a sum of two cubes?
slides.detail: 1 + 1,728 = 729 + 1,000 = 1,729. No smaller number can be split into two cubes in two different ways.

slides.heading: Not quite off the cuff
slides.text: Ramanujan had already met the number: it appears in one of his notebooks dated years before the taxi ride. Even earlier, in 1657, Frénicle de Bessy had noted the same property. The anecdote nonetheless gave us taxicab numbers, named after Hardy’s cab.
